title: Friction
question: What is friction?

principle.name: Friction
principle.formulaNote: friction = coefficient of friction × normal force. Static friction matches your push up to μs × N; once sliding, it drops to μk × N. μ has no unit and depends only on the two surfaces
principle.idea: Friction is the force that resists two surfaces sliding over each other. It grows with how hard they are pressed together (F = μ × N), hardly depends on how big the contact looks, and is what lets you walk, drive and grip anything at all.
principle.discovered: c. 1493 · Leonardo da Vinci's notebooks; 1699 · Guillaume Amontons; 1785 · Charles-Augustin de Coulomb

examples.title: Braking distance
examples.text: A car's tyres grip a dry road with μ ≈ 0.8, so from 80 km/h it can stop in about 32 m. On ice, with μ ≈ 0.1, the same stop takes about 250 m.

examples.title: Anti-lock brakes
examples.text: A skidding tyre grips about a fifth less than a rolling one and can't steer. ABS releases the brakes up to 15 times a second to keep each wheel just short of locking.

examples.title: Engine oil
examples.text: Oil dragged into the crankshaft bearings lifts the shaft on a film a few thousandths of a millimetre thick, cutting friction from about 0.1 to well under 0.01.

examples.title: Rim brakes
examples.text: Squeeze the lever with 60 N and each pad presses on the rim with about 240 N. Friction at the rim becomes about 210 N of grip at the road, and wet rims give less than half.

examples.title: Rolling beats sliding
examples.text: Bicycle tyres roll with a resistance of about 0.004 × the weight: just 3 N for a rider and bike. Dragging the same load would take over 600 N.

examples.title: Leaning on the front brake
examples.text: Braking throws a rider's weight onto the front tyre, pressing it harder into the road. More normal force means more grip, so the front brake does most of the stopping.

examples.title: The ballpoint's ball
examples.text: Friction from the paper turns the 0.7 mm ball about 4.5 times per centimetre, wiping ink onto the page. On glass it skids and nothing comes out.

examples.title: Fan bearings
examples.text: A ceiling fan's ball bearings have a friction coefficient of about 0.0015, which is why the blades keep turning long after you switch it off.

examples.title: A mixer at 18,000 rpm
examples.text: Ball bearings lose about a quarter of a watt in a mixer grinder's motor. A dry bush in their place would turn over 20 W into heat in a spot the size of a pea.

examples.title: Rope round a post
examples.text: Each turn of rope round a steel bollard multiplies its grip by about 4.8. With three turns, a 100 N pull holds more than a tonne.

hook: Friction is the force that holds before it slips. Pull a block with a spring scale and watch the grip peak then drop, stop a car on dry roads and ice, float a crankshaft on oil, hold a boat with one hand and three turns of rope, and bust the myth that pressure makes ice slippery.

explainer.title: Grip, then slip
explainer.text: Friction resists sliding. Static friction matches your pull up to a limit, μs × N; past it the surface lets go and sliding friction, μk × N, is usually smaller. μ has no unit. Tilt a ramp until a block slides and tan θ = μs. Surfaces really touch only at the tips of tiny bumps.

explainer.title: Grip on the road
explainer.text: Tyres drive, steer and stop through static friction: μ about 0.8 dry, 0.5 wet, 0.1 on ice. Braking distance is v² ÷ 2μg, so ice means eight times as far. ABS keeps wheels just short of locking. Worn tread can't clear water and the tyre aquaplanes.

explainer.title: Friction we fight
explainer.text: Rolling needs about 1% of the weight for a car, a hundredth of dragging it. Ball bearings run at μ ≈ 0.0015. An oil film floats a crankshaft off the metal, as the Stribeck curve shows. Whatever friction remains becomes heat, enough to make brake discs glow.

explainer.title: Friction we need
explainer.text: Each step pushes the ground back so the ground pushes you forward, needing μ ≈ 0.18. A pen's ball rolls only because paper grips it. Rope round a post grips exponentially, T₀ e^(μθ). Rosin makes a violin bow stick and slip hundreds of times a second.

explainer.title: Myths and limits
explainer.text: Friction doesn't depend on contact area. Ultra-smooth clean metals stick and can even cold-weld. Pressure lowers ice's melting point by only about 1.5 °C under a skate: ice is slippery because of its wet surface layer and frictional heating. Twisted graphite is superlubric, and air drag grows with speed squared.

concepts.def: The force between touching surfaces that resists them sliding over each other.
How hard two surfaces are pressed together, at right angles to them. On a flat table it equals the weight.
Friction divided by normal force. It has no unit and depends on the two surfaces.
Static friction stops sliding from starting, up to μs × N; kinetic friction acts once sliding, about μk × N.
The tiny fraction of a surface that actually touches, at the tips of its bumps. It grows with the load.
The small drag on a rolling wheel, Crr × weight: about 1% for a car tyre.
A film of oil or grease that keeps surfaces apart and cuts friction.
Jerky motion where surfaces stick, build up force, slip and stick again: violins, squeaks and earthquakes.
